L23@P0: 1 Introduction
L24@P0: Many problems in diverse areas of computer science and physics involve constructing efficient
L25@P0: representations of high-dimensional functions. Neural networks are a particular example of such
L26@P0: representations that have enjoyed great empirical success, and much effort has been dedicated to
L27@P0: understanding their expressive power - i.e. the set of functions that they can efficiently represent.
L28@P0: Analogously, tensor networks are a class of powerful representations of high-dimensional arrays
L29@P0: (tensors), for which a variety of algorithms and methods have been developed. Examples of such
L30@P0: tensor networks are tensor trains/matrix product states (MPS) [1, 2] or the hierarchical Tucker
L31@P0: decomposition [3, 4], which have found application in data compression [5–7], the simulation of
L32@P0: physical systems [8–10] and the design of machine learning algorithms [11–16]. In addition to
L33@P0: their use in numerical algorithms, tensor networks enjoy a rich analytical understanding which has
L34@P0: facilitated their use as a tool for obtaining rigorous results on the expressive power of deep learning
L35@P0: models [17–22], and fundamental insights into the structure of quantum mechanical systems [23].
L36@P0: In the context of probabilistic modeling, tensor networks have been shown to be in natural correspondence with probabilistic graphical models [24–29], as well as with Sum-Product Networks and

L38@P0-1: 33rd Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2019), Vancouver, Canada.Arithmetic Circuits [17, 30, 31]. Motivated by this correspondence, and with the goal of enhancing
L39@P1: the toolbox for deriving analytical results on the properties of machine learning algorithms, we
L40@P1: study the expressive power of various tensor-network models of discrete multivariate probability
L41@P1: distributions. The models we consider, defined in Section 2, fall into two main categories:
L42@P1: • Non-negative tensor networks, which decompose a probability mass function as a network
L43@P1: of non-negative tensors [32], as in a probabilistic graphical model [33].
L44@P1: • Born machines (BM), which model a probability mass function as the absolute value
L45@P1: squared of a real or complex function, which is itself represented as a network of real or
L46@P1: complex tensors. While Born machines have been previously employed for probabilistic
L47@P1: modeling [34–40], they have additional potential applications in the context of quantum
L48@P1: machine learning [41–44], since they arise naturally from the probabilistic interpretation of
L49@P1: quantum mechanics.
L52@P1: algorithms, while lending themselves to a rigorous theoretical analysis. In this setting non-negative
L53@P1: tensor networks encompass hidden Markov models (HMM), while Born machines include models
L54@P1: that arise from local quantum circuits of fixed depth. Our results also apply to tensor networks with
L55@P1: a tree structure, and as such can be seen as a more general comparison of the difference between
L56@P1: non-negative tensor networks and Born machines.
L57@P1: The main result of this work is a characterization of the expressive power of these tensor networks.
L58@P1: Interestingly, we prove that there exist families of probability distributions for which there are
L59@P1: unbounded separations between the resource requirements of some of these tensor-network factorizations. This allows us to show that neither HMM nor Born machines should be preferred to each other
L60@P1: in general. Moreover, we prove that using complex instead of real tensors can sometimes lead to an
L61@P1: arbitrarily large reduction in the number of parameters of the network.
L62@P1: Furthermore, we introduce a new tensor-network model of discrete multivariate probability distributions with provably better expressive power than the previously introduced models. This tensor
L63@P1: network, which retains an efficient learning algorithm, is referred to as a locally purified state (LPS)
L64@P1: due to its origin in the classical simulation of quantum systems [45–48]. We demonstrate through
L65@P1: numerical experiments on both random probability distributions as well as realistic data sets that our
L66@P1: theoretical findings are relevant in practice - i.e. that LPS should be considered over HMM and Born
L67@P1: machines for probabilistic modeling.
L68@P1: This paper is structured as follows: The models we consider are introduced in Section 2. Their
L69@P1: relation with HMM and quantum circuits is made explicit in Section 3. The main results on expressive
L70@P1: power are presented in Section 4. Section 5 then introduces learning algorithms for these tensor
L71@P1: networks, and the results of numerical experiments are provided in Section 6.
L72@P1: 2 Tensor-network models of probability distributions
L73@P1: Consider a multivariate probability mass function P(X1, . . . , XN ) over N discrete random variables
L74@P1: {Xi} taking values in {1, . . . , d}. This probability mass function is naturally represented as a multidimensional array, or tensor, with N indices, each of which can take d values. As such, we use the
L75@P1: notation P to refer simultaneously to both the probability mass function and the equivalent tensor
L76@P1: representation. More specifically, for each configuration X1, . . . , XN the tensor element PX1,...,XN
L77@P1: stores the probability P(X1, . . . , XN ). Note that as P is a representation of a probability mass
L78@P1: function, it is a tensor with non-negative entries summing to one.
L79@P1: Here we are interested in the case where N is large. Since the number of elements of this tensor scales
L80@P1: exponentially with N, it is quickly impossible to store. In cases where there is some structure to the
L81@P1: variables, one may use a compact representation of P which exploits this structure, such as Bayesian
L82@P1: networks or Markov random fields defined on a graph. In the following we consider models, known
L83@P1: as tensor networks, in which a tensor T is factorized into the contraction of multiple smaller tensors.
L84@P1: As long as T is non-negative, one can model P as P = T /ZT , where ZT =

L499@P7: 6.1 Random tensor factorizations
L500@P7: We first generate random probability mass functions P by generating a tensor with elements chosen
L501@P7: uniformly in [0, 1] and normalizing it. We then minimize the KL-divergence D(P||T /ZT ), where T
L502@P7: is the tensor defined by an MPS, BM or LPS with given rank r. We choose LPS to have a purification
L503@P7: dimension of 2. Details of the optimization are available in the supplementary material.

L508@P7: Results are presented in Fig. 3 for a 20 × 20 matrix and a tensor with 8 binary variables. They show
L509@P7: that complex BM as well as real and complex LPS generically provide a better approximation to a
L510@P7: tensor than an MPS or real BM, for fixed rank as well as for fixed number of real parameters.
L511@P7-8: 86.2 Maximum likelihood estimation on realistic data sets
L512@P8: We now investigate how well the different tensor-network representations are able to learn from
L513@P8: realistic data sets. We train MPSR≥0, BMR, BMC, LPSR and LPSC (of purification dimension 2) using
L514@P8: the algorithm of Section 5 on different data sets of categorical variables. Since we are interested in the
L515@P8: expressive power of the different representations we use the complete data sets and no regularization.
L516@P8: Additional results on generalization performance are included in the supplementary material.

L522@P8: The results in Fig. 4 show the best negative log-likelihood per sample obtained for each tensor
L523@P8: network of fixed rank. As a comparison we also include the best negative log-likelihood obtained
L524@P8: from an HMM trained using the Baum-Welch algorithm [61, 62], as well as the best possible Bayesian
L525@P8: network without hidden variables, where the network graph is learned from the data [62]. We observe
L526@P8: that despite the different algorithm choice, the performance of HMM and MPSR≥0are similar, as we
L527@P8: could expect from their relationship. On all data sets, BM and LPS lead to significant improvements
L528@P8: for the same rank over MPSR≥0.
L529@P8: 7 Conclusion
L530@P8: We have characterized the expressive power of various tensor-network models of probability distributions, in the process enhancing the scope and applicability of the tensor-network toolbox within
L531@P8: the broader context of learning algorithms. In particular, our analysis has concrete implications
L532@P8: for model selection, suggesting that in generic settings LPS should be preferred over both hidden
L533@P8: Markov models and Born machines. Furthermore, our results prove that unexpectedly the use of
L534@P8: complex tensors over real tensors can lead to an unbounded expressive advantage in particular network
L535@P8: architectures. Additionally, this work contributes to the growing body of rigorous results concerning
L536@P8: the expressive power of learning models, which have been obtained via tensor-network techniques. A
L537@P8: formal understanding of the expressive power of state-of-the-art learning models is often elusive; it is
L538@P8: hoped that both the techniques and spirit of this work can be used to add momentum to this program.
L539@P8: Finally, through the formal relationship of LPS and Born machines to quantum circuits, our work
L540@P8: provides a concrete foundation for both the development and analysis of quantum machine learning
L541@P8: algorithms for near-term quantum devices.

L1829@P25: 4 Conclusion
L1830@P25: In this work we have demonstrated how belief propagation (BP) can be used to bring an
L1831@P25: arbitrary tensor network state (TNS) into a gauge commonly used in the tensor network literature — which we refer to as the Vidal gauge but has previously been referred to as the
L1832@P25: super-orthogonal or quasi-canonical gauge — where multiple local orthogonality conditions
L1833@P25: are (approximately) satisfied. We showed that it can be viewed as a simplified version of
L1834@P25: a gauging method previously introduced in Refs. [132, 134]. We have benchmarked our
L1835@P25-26: ‘belief propagation gauging’ algorithm, demonstrating that it can be faster than existing al26SciPost Physics 5 ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

L331@P7: 4. Hidden Quantum Models
L332@P7: In this section we define the Hidden Quantum Markov Model (HQMM), based on the
L333@P7: notion of quantum operation. The spirit underlying our definition follows exactly the
L334@P7: same lines as the definition of a HMM. In a HMM (HQMM) there is an underlying
L335@P7: Markovian (Quantum) process which rules the probability of the symbols generated.
